1009.title: No water, no moon
1009.hook: the nun Chiyono's bucket bottom breaks, the moon's reflection vanishes, and she awakens
1009.howItsDone: Chiyono's story and her verse about the broken bucket are retold in Zen collections, alongside other stories of awakening that come in an ordinary moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ryokan plays, curled up in the straw at dawn. Your line was still hiding. What did you play, and did you stay in it? Day one thousand nine.

An old wooden bucket, its staves held together by a hoop of bamboo. A nun carries it out at night to fetch water. She fills it, and as she walks back she glances down: the full moon is floating in the water, bright and round, held right there in her bucket. Then the bamboo hoop snaps. The staves spring apart, the bottom drops out, and the water rushes onto the ground. The moon in the bucket is gone. Tradition says that in that moment, the nun Chiyono woke up. Today's word: no water.
screen: `THE MOON IN HER BUCKET.` → `THE HOOP SNAPS.` → `THE WATER IS GONE.`

segments.voice: First, Chiyono. She comes to us through Zen stories as a woman who practiced for a long time, working and sitting at a temple, without the breakthrough she hoped for. Tellings differ about her life before; they agree about the bucket. Second, the moon in the water. Buddhist writing uses this picture to describe things that look solid and aren't. The moon in a bucket looks real. It's bright. You could almost scoop it out. But it's a reflection, and it lasts only as long as the water stays still and the bucket holds. Third, the bottom falls out. Tradition gives Chiyono a short verse about that night. In plain English it says, roughly: I tried this way and that to keep the old bucket together, until the bottom fell out. Where no water stays, no moon lives. Read that way, her years of effort were the bamboo hoop. She kept holding things together, the bucket, the practice, the picture of what awakening should look like. When the hoop gave way, what she'd been holding so carefully turned out not to be what she was looking for. Fourth, what's not lost. The story never says the moon left the sky. Only the copy went, with the water. Some readers hear the self in that bucket, a reflection carried carefully from place to place. Others hear every idea of awakening, which has to spill before awakening can happen. The story leaves room for both, and the real moon stays where it always was.
screen: `CHIYONO AND THE OLD BUCKET.` · `THE MOON IN THE WATER.` · `THE BOTTOM FALLS OUT.` · `ONLY THE REFLECTION IS GONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch water spill, or remember it. If there's a glass near you, pour a little from one cup into another, or into a sink, and watch it go. If not, remember rain sliding off a roof, or a wave pulling back from the sand. Notice the moment the water leaves its shape. Then turn to your breath, and let each out-breath spill the same way, without holding anything together. Nothing to keep. Nothing to carry. The bell holds the time.
No water. Chiyono's bucket breaks, the water spills, and the moon's reflection is gone, while the moon itself stays in the sky. Today's word.
Your line: the bottom fell out. Today, watch water spill, from a tap, a cup or a puddle, and when something you've been holding together gives way, look up before you clean up. Day one thousand nine.

1010.title: Lay meditation
1010.hook: Ledi Sayadaw in Burma teaches meditation to laypeople, not only monks
1010.howItsDone: In Theravada countries and beyond, lay Buddhists now attend meditation retreats and centers, and some lineages trace this lay practice back through teachers such as Ledi Sayadaw and Saya Thetgyi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chiyono's bucket, the bottom falling out under the moon. Your line was the bottom fell out. What gave way, and what did you see when it did? Day one thousand ten.

Who is meditation for? In Burma, in Ledi Sayadaw's day, the usual answer, as accounts tell it, was the monks. Lay people offered food, kept the precepts, made merit, and left the long hours of sitting to those in robes. Ledi Sayadaw was a learned monk, and he started giving a different answer. Farmers could do this. Shopkeepers could do this. Parents with no spare time could do this. He wrote short guides in plain Burmese and sent them out into the towns and villages. Today's word: lay meditation.
screen: `WHO IS MEDITATION FOR?` → `THE MONKS, MOSTLY.` → `LEDI SAYS: EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: First, the worry behind it. Accounts of Ledi Sayadaw describe a teacher afraid the practice could shrink into something people only read about, kept alive by a few. His answer was to widen the circle, to put the practice in more hands, not fewer. Second, the tools. He wrote practical guides in the everyday language people actually spoke, on keeping attention on the breath and on seeing body and mind change from moment to moment. The Pali word for that seeing is vipassana: insight, seeing clearly. It wasn't a new teaching. The instructions on mindfulness of breathing and of the body are in the old suttas. What was new was who he handed them to. Third, the farmer. A story told in this lineage: a rice farmer named Saya Thetgyi learned from Ledi and became a teacher himself, a lay man teaching lay people in his own village. From him the teaching passed on through other lay teachers, and teachers in this line say it now reaches meditation halls far from Burma, where lay people of every kind sit side by side. Fourth, what it changed, and what it didn't. Ledi didn't set monastic life aside; he stayed a monk. He simply said the door was wider than people thought. The sitting wasn't a reward for having left the world. It was something a person could carry into the world, in the time between the fields and the market, between one chore and the next.
screen: `A FEAR THE PRACTICE WOULD SHRINK.` · `PLAIN GUIDES IN PLAIN BURMESE.` · `A FARMER BECOMES A TEACHER.` · `THE DOOR IS WIDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn it so you could teach it. Sit comfortably and breathe in and out through the nose. Notice the touch of the air just at the nostrils as it comes in, and as it goes out. That's the whole instruction. When your mind wanders off, come back to the touch. Keep it simple enough that you could explain it to anyone in one sentence. Later today, if someone asks, you could show them the same thing. The bell holds the time.
Lay meditation. Ledi Sayadaw's teaching that insight practice belongs to farmers and shopkeepers as well as monks. Today's word.
Your line: for everyone. Today, teach one person to breathe: one slow breath, feeling the air at the nose, the way a farmer once learned it from a monk. Day one thousand ten.

1011.title: Noting spreads
1011.hook: Mahasi Sayadaw's method of noting travels far beyond Burma
1011.howItsDone: In Mahasi-style retreats, meditators alternate periods of sitting, noting the rise and fall of the abdomen, with slow walking, noting each part of each step, often for whole days in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lay meditation: Ledi Sayadaw opening insight practice to farmers and shopkeepers. Your line was for everyone. Who did you teach to breathe? Day one thousand eleven.

Rising. Falling. Rising. Falling. Two words, said silently, over and over, in a meditation hall in Burma, or in a hall on another continent. A person sits, sometimes with a hand resting on the belly. As the belly lifts with the in-breath, they note: rising. As it sinks: falling. Then a sound arrives from outside. Hearing, hearing. An itch on the cheek. Itching. A sudden memory of breakfast. Thinking. Then back to the belly. That's the method a Burmese monk, Mahasi Sayadaw, taught, and that's today's word: noting spreads.
screen: `RISING. FALLING.` → `HEARING, HEARING.` → `THINKING. BACK TO THE BELLY.`

segments.voice: First, the home base. Mahasi Sayadaw built his teaching on the old instructions in the Satipatthana Sutta to be mindful of body, feelings, mind and the things the mind meets. He made it simple to start: choose one place to return to, the rise and fall of the belly, and come back there again and again. Second, the label. Whatever pulls attention away gets a soft, plain word. Not a judgment. Not a story. Just a name for what's happening: hearing, itching, wanting, worrying. The note is made silently, in the mind, and teachers in his line describe it as light, a whisper rather than a shout. Naming a sound as hearing keeps you from building a whole argument about the neighbor's car. The label catches the moment before the story starts. Third, walking. Practice in Mahasi centers doesn't stop when you stand up. Students walk slowly back and forth, noting each step: lifting, moving, placing. They alternate sitting and walking through the day, so attention carries from the cushion to the floor to the dining hall. Fourth, how it traveled. Mahasi's students, monks and lay people both, carried the method to centers in other countries, and teachers there adapted it. Some keep careful labels for everything. Some use them only when the mind gets lost, then drop them. The method turned out to be plain enough to travel and flexible enough to change, which is how the words rising, falling came to be whispered in halls a long way from where Mahasi taught.
screen: `A HOME BASE: RISING, FALLING.` · `A SOFT LABEL, NOT A JUDGMENT.` · `LIFTING, MOVING, PLACING.` · `PLAIN ENOUGH TO TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note, gently. Sit, and find the movement of your belly as you breathe; resting a hand there can help. As it rises, silently say rising. As it falls, falling. When something pulls you away, give it one soft word: hearing, thinking, itching, planning. Then come back to rising, falling. No need to note perfectly, and no need to note everything. A whisper is enough. The bell holds the time.
Noting spreads. Mahasi Sayadaw's method: rising, falling, and a soft label for whatever pulls you away, carried by his students far beyond Burma. Today's word.
Your line: rising, falling. Today, note for five minutes, sitting or walking, one soft word at a time: rising, falling, lifting, placing. Day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: The forest wanderer
1012.hook: Ajahn Mun walks the Thai forests, reviving the strict forest life
1012.howItsDone: Monks in the Thai forest tradition live in forest monasteries, walk for alms each morning, and some take on the dhutanga practices, sometimes wandering for a season in what Thai Buddhists call thudong.

segments.voice: Yesterday, noting spreads: Mahasi Sayadaw's soft labels. Your line was rising, falling. When did one plain word catch a story before it started? Day one thousand twelve.

Dawn under a tree. A monk climbs out from beneath a cloth umbrella hung from a branch, a net around it against the mosquitoes. He shoulders his bowl and walks barefoot into the nearest village. People put rice in the bowl. He takes what's given, walks back into the trees, and eats once. Then he sits, and walks, and sits. In a few days or weeks he'll move on to another forest, and another. The stories told about him mention wild animals, fever and long nights of fear. His name was Ajahn Mun, and today's word is dhutanga.
screen: `A NET, A BOWL, A TREE.` → `ONE MEAL, THEN BACK TO THE FOREST.` → `ALWAYS MOVING ON.`

segments.voice: First, what he took on. The Pali tradition describes a set of strict practices, dhutanga, that a monk may choose: living in the forest, eating only food received on alms round, eating from the bowl alone, wearing robes of cast-off cloth, sleeping at the foot of a tree. They're optional. Tradition says the Buddha praised them and refused to make them required. Ajahn Mun chose them, and kept them, and that's what people mean when they say he revived the forest life in Thailand. Second, why the forest. There's no comfort out there to hide in. When fear comes up at night, you sit with fear. When hunger comes, you sit with hunger. Accounts of his life, written down by his students, tell of fear met with steady meditation until it passed. The forest wasn't scenery. It was the teacher that wouldn't let him look away. Third, the students. Monks who wanted to train with him had to find him first, and he kept moving. Those who caught up learned as much from watching as from talks: how he walked, ate, swept and sat. The Thai forest teachers who came after him speak of him as a root teacher. Fourth, what wandering meant. It wasn't running away. It was a way of keeping nothing: no fixed hut to defend, no reputation to manage, no comfortable corner to settle into. Just the next step, the bowl, and the mind as it is right now.
screen: `DHUTANGA: STRICT PRACTICES, CHOSEN.` · `NO COMFORT TO HIDE IN.` · `STUDENTS HAD TO FIND HIM.` · `A WAY OF KEEPING NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a forest walk, wherever you are. If you can, stand near a tree, or a window with a tree in view. If not, bring one to mind. Walk a few slow steps, or simply stand still. Let your attention widen to whatever is around you, and listen to it as if it were forest sound: wind, a bird, a far-off engine. If restlessness or a little fear shows up, let it walk with you. The bell holds the time.
Dhutanga. The strict practices a monk may choose, like living in the forest and eating once a day, which Ajahn Mun kept. Today's word.
Your line: just the next step. Today, walk among trees mindfully, even a single tree on your street, and let your feet go slowly. Day one thousand twelve.

1013.title: A forest student
1013.hook: Ajahn Chah, Ajahn Mun's student in spirit, whose forest monastery welcomed Western monks
1013.howItsDone: Monasteries in Ajahn Chah's lineage, in Thailand and in other countries, follow the forest routine of alms round, work and meditation, and welcome lay visitors and guests who wish to stay and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ajahn Mun with his bowl and a tree for a roof. Your line was just the next step. Where did your feet slow down? Day one thousand thirteen.

A young man from the West stands at the gate of a forest monastery in Thailand, newly ordained or hoping to be. He doesn't speak the language. He doesn't know the chants. He isn't sure how to wrap a robe or where to leave his sandals. The teacher there could easily tell him to come back when he knows more. Instead, as the story is told, he's let in and put to work: sweeping leaves off the paths, hauling water, walking for alms with everyone else. The teacher was Ajahn Chah. Today's word: acariya.
screen: `A STRANGER AT THE GATE.` → `NO LANGUAGE, NO CHANTS.` → `LET IN AND HANDED A BROOM.`

segments.voice: First, a student in spirit. Tradition says Ajahn Chah spent only a short time with Ajahn Mun, yet that meeting stayed with him. Afterward he wandered and practiced in the forests the way Mun had, and in time settled in a forest near his home village, where a monastery grew up around him. That's why he's called Mun's student in spirit: not long years at his side, but the same forest way. Second, his way of teaching. Accounts describe Ajahn Chah speaking in plain village language, with jokes and everyday pictures: a glass of muddy water settling, a leaf stirred by the wind. When students complained about the heat, the food or each other, he would turn the complaint around. The trouble, he suggested, wasn't the heat. It was the wanting it to be different. Third, the welcome. Western monks came, and he didn't build them an easier track. They ate the same food, kept the same hours, swept the same paths and sat through the same restless nights. In time a monastery was set up near his own, Wat Pah Nanachat, where newcomers from abroad could train with teaching in English. Fourth, what welcome means here. It isn't lowering the bar. It's opening the gate, and then walking beside the newcomer through the same hard days. The forest welcomed them, and it didn't change for them. Monasteries started later by his Western students carry the same pattern into other countries.
screen: `A STUDENT IN SPIRIT.` · `PLAIN WORDS, VILLAGE PICTURES.` · `NO SEPARATE, EASIER TRACK.` · `AN OPEN GATE, THE SAME PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember being new. Settle, and breathe. Bring back a time you were the newcomer: a job, a school, a country, a family dinner where you knew nobody. Remember what helped. A person who showed you where things were. Someone who didn't make you feel slow. Breathe with that memory for a moment. Then bring to mind someone who's new in your life right now, at work, on your street, in a group. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Acariya. The Pali word for teacher, the root of the Thai title ajahn, given to teachers like Ajahn Chah who welcomed students from abroad. Today's word.
Your line: the forest welcomed them. Today, welcome one newcomer: show someone where things are, and walk beside them for a little while. Day one thousand thirteen.

1014.title: The garden of liberation
1014.hook: Buddhadasa's forest monastery in southern Thailand and his plain teaching
1014.howItsDone: Suan Mokkh still welcomes visitors and holds meditation retreats, and Buddhadasa's talks, published in plain Thai, are read by Thai Buddhists and in translation elsewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, acariya, the forest student: Ajahn Chah opening the gate to newcomers. Your line was the forest welcomed them. Who did you walk beside? Day one thousand fourteen.

Books packed, a monk who has been studying in Bangkok heads home. Not in defeat. He's decided the big city temples, with their exams and ranks, aren't where he'll find what he's looking for. Back in the south of Thailand, near the town he grew up in, he settles in a quiet, overgrown patch of forest and gives it a name: Suan Mokkh, the garden of liberation. The monk is known as Buddhadasa. He wanted to talk about the Buddha's teaching in words that anyone, a farmer, a student, a clerk, could use that afternoon. Today's word: Buddhadasa.
screen: `HE LEAVES THE CITY TEMPLES.` → `A QUIET FOREST IN THE SOUTH.` → `SUAN MOKKH: THE GARDEN OF LIBERATION.`

segments.voice: First, two languages. Buddhadasa taught that religious words can be heard in two ways. There's everyday language, the words as people usually take them. And there's what he called Dhamma language, the same words heard inwardly. Rebirth, in everyday language, can mean being born again after death. In Dhamma language, he said, it can also mean the self being born again and again in the mind, every time we grab hold of I and mine. He didn't tell people to throw the first meaning away. He asked them to hear the second one too. Second, plain words. He spoke to farmers, officials and students in ordinary Thai. At Suan Mokkh he put teachings on signs among the trees and paintings on the walls, so a visitor could learn just by walking around. Third, cooling, here and now. The old texts picture nibbana as a fire going out. Buddhadasa liked the picture of cooling, and he taught that a taste of it can come in ordinary life, whenever grasping drops for a moment, not only at the end of a long road. Fourth, not everyone agreed. Some Thai Buddhists felt his readings went too far from the traditional ones. Others found them freeing. He kept teaching plainly, and the signs among the trees stayed up for anyone who walked in, a farmer or a professor, to read on the way past.
screen: `EVERYDAY LANGUAGE, DHAMMA LANGUAGE.` · `SIGNS AMONG THE TREES.` · `COOLING, HERE AND NOW.` · `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plain words. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing you understand well: how to cook rice, why you love a certain song, a rule of a game you play. In your head, explain it as if to a curious child. Short words. One picture. No showing off. Notice where you reach for a fancy word, and swap it for a plain one. Then let the breath be plain too: in, and out. The bell holds the time.
Buddhadasa. The Thai monk who taught the Buddha's teaching in plain words at his forest monastery, Suan Mokkh, the garden of liberation. Today's word.
Your line: plain words. Today, explain one thing plainly to someone, with short words and a single picture. Day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: Ambedkar's conversion
1015.hook: at Nagpur, Dr B. R. Ambedkar and a great crowd of Dalits take refuge
1015.howItsDone: Ambedkarite Buddhists mark the anniversary of the Nagpur conversion each year, and crowds gather at the site in Nagpur, now called Deekshabhoomi, to take the refuges and remember Ambedkar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garden of liberation: Buddhadasa's forest and his two languages. Your line was plain words. What did you explain, and to whom? Day one thousand fifteen.

An open ground in Nagpur, a city in the middle of India. A great crowd, stretching back across the ground. In the crowd are Dalits, people the caste system had called untouchable: kept from common wells, from temple doors, from classrooms. At the front stands a lawyer and scholar, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, who helped draft the constitution of independent India and spent his life fighting caste discrimination. Today he is not here to argue a case. He is here to take refuge in the Buddha. Today's word: Ambedkar's conversion.
screen: `AN OPEN GROUND IN NAGPUR.` → `A CROWD OF DALITS.` → `AMBEDKAR AT THE FRONT.`

segments.voice: First, his own life. Ambedkar was born into a Dalit family. Accounts of his childhood say he had to sit apart at school and couldn't drink from the common water unless someone poured it for him. He studied anyway, in India and abroad, and became a lawyer, an economist and a leader of his people. Second, a long search. Long before this day, he had said publicly that he would leave the religion he was born into, and he studied more than one path before choosing. He chose the Buddha's, and he gave his own reasons: a teaching that, as he read it, rested on reason, compassion and the equal worth of every person. This is his story and his reading, told here as his. Hindus have their own and varied answers to caste, and Hindu reformers have fought untouchability too. Third, the ceremony. Accounts say Ambedkar first received the refuges and precepts himself from a senior Buddhist monk. Then he turned to the crowd and led them through the refuges in Pali, line by line: Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge; then the Dhamma; then the Sangha. A whole field of voices repeating after one. Fourth, the week. It began with Chiyono's bucket, the water gone and the moon still in the sky. Ledi Sayadaw opened meditation to everyone. Mahasi taught rising, falling. Ajahn Mun wandered the forests, Ajahn Chah welcomed newcomers through the gate, and Buddhadasa spoke in plain words. And today, on an open ground, a crowd that had been refused dignity for generations stands up and chooses it.
